note: Research behind RESEARCH-grade claims on PORTFOLIO / CONSTRUCT. Each entry says what the guide uses it for and how strong the evidence is.

sources.cite: Markowitz, H. (1952). Portfolio Selection. Journal of Finance 7(1).
sources.use: Portfolio variance depends on covariances, not just each asset's risk.

sources.cite: Carver, R. (2015). Systematic Trading. Harriman House. (Also Leveraged Trading, 2019; Advanced Futures Trading Strategies, 2023.)
sources.use: Diversification multiplier 1/sqrt(w'Hw) with negative correlations floored at 0 and a cap; handcrafted weights; volatility targeting; half-Kelly.

sources.cite: Booth, D. & Fama, E. (1992). Diversification Returns and Asset Contributions. Financial Analysts Journal 48(3).
sources.use: Compound return ≈ arithmetic return − variance/2; a diversified portfolio's compound return exceeds the weighted compound returns of its parts.

sources.cite: Luenberger, D. (1998). Investment Science, ch. 15 'Volatility pumping'. Oxford University Press.
sources.use: The coin-flip asset with zero expected log growth that becomes a growing portfolio when rebalanced against cash.

sources.cite: Fernholz, R. & Shay, B. (1982). Stochastic Portfolio Theory and Stock Market Equilibrium. Journal of Finance 37(2).
sources.use: Excess growth rate of a constant-weight portfolio = ½(Σwσ² − σ_p²).

sources.cite: Willenbrock, S. (2011). Diversification Return, Portfolio Rebalancing, and the Commodity Return Puzzle. Financial Analysts Journal 67(4).
sources.use: The diversification return is earned by rebalancing; it is not a free return premium of any one asset.

sources.cite: Hallerbach, W. (2014). Disentangling Rebalancing Return. Journal of Asset Management 15.
sources.use: Caveat: rebalancing does not guarantee beating the best single asset; the bonus needs volatile, weakly correlated assets and low costs.

sources.cite: Sharpe, W. (1994). The Sharpe Ratio. Journal of Portfolio Management 21(1).
sources.use: A standalone Sharpe ratio ignores correlation with what you already hold; the best addition is not necessarily the highest-Sharpe fund.

sources.cite: Standard mean-variance result; derived explicitly in 'Incremental Sharpe and other performance ratios' (arXiv:1807.09864, 2018).
sources.use: A marginal allocation raises the portfolio Sharpe iff SR_new > ρ·SR_portfolio, equivalently the new stream has positive alpha (μ_new > β·μ_portfolio) against the portfolio.

sources.cite: Bailey, D. & López de Prado, M. (2013). The Strategy Approval Decision: A Sharpe Ratio Indifference Curve Approach. Algorithmic Finance 2(1).
sources.use: Approving strategies on past Sharpe alone is suboptimal; correlation to the existing book sets the hurdle.

sources.cite: Multi-Strat Mark (practitioner commentary) — the 'napkin math' hurdle for adding a return stream.
sources.use: Popular statement of the same rule. The guide uses the exact mean-variance form (Sharpe and correlation, or return and beta).

sources.cite: DeMiguel, V., Garlappi, L. & Uppal, R. (2009). Optimal Versus Naive Diversification: How Inefficient is the 1/N Portfolio Strategy? Review of Financial Studies 22(5).
sources.use: Across 14 models and 7 datasets none beat 1/N consistently out of sample: estimation error swamps optimisation gains.

sources.cite: Michaud, R. (1989). The Markowitz Optimization Enigma: Is 'Optimized' Optimal? Financial Analysts Journal 45(1).
sources.use: Mean-variance optimisers maximise estimation error; resampling averages it out.

sources.cite: Ledoit, O. & Wolf, M. (2004). A Well-Conditioned Estimator for Large-Dimensional Covariance Matrices. Journal of Multivariate Analysis 88(2).
sources.use: Shrinking the sample covariance toward a structured target improves out-of-sample portfolios.

sources.cite: Maillard, S., Roncalli, T. & Teïletche, J. (2010). The Properties of Equally Weighted Risk Contribution Portfolios. Journal of Portfolio Management 36(4).
sources.use: Equal-risk-contribution portfolios sit between minimum variance and 1/N.

sources.cite: Jaconetti, C., Kinniry, F. & Zilbering, Y. (2010). Best Practices for Portfolio Rebalancing. Vanguard Research.
sources.use: Rebalancing is mainly risk control; threshold (e.g. 5%) and annual/semiannual monitoring are reasonable; frequent rebalancing mostly adds cost.

sources.cite: Bouchey, P., Nemtchinov, V., Paulsen, A. & Stein, D. (2012). Volatility Harvesting: Why Does Diversifying and Rebalancing Create Portfolio Growth? Journal of Wealth Management 15(2).
sources.use: Empirical rebalancing bonus is largest for volatile, low-correlation assets.

sources.cite: Kelly, J. (1956). A New Interpretation of Information Rate. Bell System Technical Journal 35(4); Thorp, E. (2006). The Kelly Criterion in Blackjack, Sports Betting and the Stock Market.
sources.use: Growth-optimal leverage = excess return / variance; growth falls past it and is zero at twice Kelly.

sources.cite: Moreira, A. & Muir, T. (2017). Volatility-Managed Portfolios. Journal of Finance 72(4); Harvey, C. et al. (2018). The Impact of Volatility Targeting. Journal of Portfolio Management 45(1).
sources.use: Scaling exposure by inverse recent volatility reduces tail risk and vol-of-vol; Sharpe gains are clear for equities, weaker elsewhere.

sources.cite: Cederburg, S., O'Doherty, M., Wang, F. & Yan, X. (2020). On the Performance of Volatility-Managed Portfolios. Journal of Financial Economics 138(1).
sources.use: Counter-evidence: out-of-sample, volatility management does not systematically beat the unmanaged portfolio — treat it as risk control first.

sources.cite: Longin, F. & Solnik, B. (2001). Extreme Correlation of International Equity Markets. Journal of Finance 56(2).
sources.use: Correlations rise in bear markets: diversification is weakest when it is needed most.

sources.cite: Hurst, B., Ooi, Y. H. & Pedersen, L. (2017). A Century of Evidence on Trend-Following Investing. Journal of Portfolio Management 44(1); Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012). Time Series Momentum. JFE 104(2).
sources.use: Trend following has historically done well in the worst equity drawdowns ('crisis alpha').

sources.cite: Israelov, R. (2017). Pathetic Protection: The Elusive Benefits of Protective Puts. Journal of Alternative Investments 21(2).
sources.use: Long-vol / put protection is expensive to carry; size it as insurance, not as an alpha source (see OPTIONS LAB · PPUT calibration).
